blocks.content: A user clicks checkout and nine hundred milliseconds later the page finally loads. Nobody's happy, but you don't even know why yet.
That one request touched an API gateway, a cart service, an inventory service, and a payment service. Somewhere in that chain, most of the nine hundred milliseconds disappeared. Which service ate it?

Your logs can tell you each service ran without crashing. Your metrics can tell you the payment service is averaging 700ms lately. Neither one can show you, for this exact request, exactly which hop was slow and by how much.
Distributed tracing follows a single request across every service it touches, recording how long each hop took, so you can point at the exact slow piece instead of guessing.
1. Introduction
If you've looked at the three pillars of observability before, you already know traces sit alongside logs and metrics. This topic is the deep dive into how tracing actually works under the hood.

The core problem tracing solves is simple to state and painful to live without: in a system made of many services, a single user request fans out into many internal calls, and when it's slow, you need to know which one of those calls was the culprit.

["Logs tell you what happened inside one service","Metrics tell you how a service is doing in aggregate over time","Traces tell you where one specific request spent its time, across every service it touched"]
items: Logs tell you what happened inside one service
Metrics tell you how a service is doing in aggregate over time
Traces tell you where one specific request spent its time, across every service it touched

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351175-712762271.png
blocks.alt: Logs answer what happened, metrics answer how much, traces answer where the time went

blocks.title: This is a per-request tool
blocks.content: Tracing shines when you already know something is slow and need to find the one service or call responsible. It's the microscope, not the smoke detector.
2. Traces and spans
A trace represents one end to end request, from the moment it enters your system to the moment a response goes back out.

A trace is made up of multiple spans. Each span represents one unit of work inside that request, like one service handling its part of the job, or one database call, or one call out to a third party API.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351176-447141498.png
blocks.alt: A single trace made up of a gateway span, a cart span, an inventory span, and a payment span

blocks.content: 2.1 What a span actually records
Strip a span down to its essentials and it's not complicated. It records when it started, how long it took, and a reference back to whichever span caused it to happen.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351177-511781368.png
blocks.alt: One span recording its start time, its duration, and its parent span id

blocks.content: ["A unique span id","A start time and a duration","The name of the operation, like cart.addItem or db.query","A reference to its parent span id","Optional attributes and tags, like a customer id or an HTTP status code"]
items: A unique span id
A start time and a duration
The name of the operation, like cart.addItem or db.query
A reference to its parent span id
Optional attributes and tags, like a customer id or an HTTP status code

blocks.title: A span isn't a log line
blocks.content: A log line is a message about a moment in time. A span is a measured duration with a clear start and end, plus a place in a tree. That's what makes waterfall views possible.
3. The parent child span tree

Every span except the very first one in a trace has a parent. The gateway span is the root. It calls the cart service, so the cart span's parent is the gateway span. The cart service calls its own database, so that query span's parent is the cart span.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351806-482898658.png
blocks.alt: A root gateway span with cart and payment child spans, and a database query span nested under cart

blocks.content: Chain all these parent pointers together and you get a tree, not just a flat list. That tree is what tells a real story: which service called which, in what order, and how deep the call chain actually went for this specific request.
3.1 Why the tree matters more than the list
blocks.text: 3.1 Why the tree matters more than the list

blocks.content: A flat list of spans would tell you a trace had four spans and how long each took. A tree tells you which span waited on which other span, so you can see whether the payment span was slow on its own, or slow because it was waiting on a child call that was slow.

["The root span's duration is roughly the total time the whole request took","A child span's duration is time spent inside that one call","Time not covered by any child span is time the parent spent doing its own work"]
items: The root span's duration is roughly the total time the whole request took
A child span's duration is time spent inside that one call
Time not covered by any child span is time the parent spent doing its own work

blocks.title: Two spans with the same duration can mean very different things
blocks.content: One span that's slow because of its own CPU work looks identical in a table to one that's slow because it's waiting on a child. The tree is what tells them apart.
4. Propagating trace context across services
None of this tree building works unless every service involved knows it's part of the same trace. That's what trace context propagation is for.

When service A calls service B, it passes the trace id and its own current span id along in the request, almost always as HTTP headers. Service B reads those values, creates its own span with that trace id, and sets its parent to the span id it just received.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351809-485042515.png
blocks.alt: A trace id and span id being passed from the cart service to the inventory service inside a request header

blocks.content: 4.1 What actually travels in the header
blocks.text: 4.1 What actually travels in the header

blocks.content: ["Trace id the same id shared by every span in this one request, start to finish","Current span id becomes the parent id for whatever span the next service creates","Sampling flag tells downstream services whether this particular trace is being recorded in full"]
items: Trace id the same id shared by every span in this one request, start to finish
Current span id becomes the parent id for whatever span the next service creates
Sampling flag tells downstream services whether this particular trace is being recorded in full

blocks.title: Miss one hop and the trace breaks
blocks.content: If any service in the chain forwards the request without copying these headers along, the trace splits into two disconnected pieces. This is the single most common bug in real tracing setups, usually hiding in a raw HTTP client call that skips the tracing library.
5. The W3C Trace Context standard

Early on, every tracing vendor invented its own header format for this. Jaeger had one, Zipkin had another, and none of them understood each other's headers. That meant mixing tools across a company was painful.

The W3C Trace Context standard fixed that by defining one common header format, called traceparent, that any tracing tool or library can read and write. It's the reason a Java service using one tracing library and a Node service using a completely different one can still end up in the same trace.
5.1 Reading a traceparent header
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351809-480356513.png
blocks.alt: The traceparent header broken into version, trace id, parent span id, and flags

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Meaning"],"rows":[["00","Version of the traceparent format"],["4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736","The trace id, shared by every span in this trace"],["00f067aa0ba902b7","The id of the span that made this call, becomes the parent id downstream"],["01","Flags, here meaning this trace is sampled and should be recorded"]]}

blocks.title: This is transport, not storage
blocks.content: Traceparent only standardizes how the ids travel between services in a request header. Where those spans actually get stored and displayed is still up to whichever backend you point them at, like Jaeger or Zipkin.
6. Sampling

Recording a full trace for every single request sounds ideal until you do the math at real traffic. A service handling ten thousand requests a second generating a full span tree for every one of them is a lot of data to ship, store, and pay for.
6.1 Head based sampling

The simplest approach decides at the start of a request, before anything is known about how it'll go, whether to trace it at all. Keep 1 in 100 requests, say, and drop the rest before they generate any spans.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351810-387366104.png
blocks.alt: Out of 100 requests, only a small percentage get fully traced and the rest are dropped

blocks.content: 6.2 Tail based sampling

The smarter approach waits until the request is actually finished, looks at how it went, and then decides. Keep every trace that had an error. Keep every trace that was unusually slow. For everything else, boring and fast, keep only a small sample.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351810-107149721.png
blocks.alt: A fast clean request usually dropped, but an errored or unusually slow request always kept

blocks.content: ["Head based cheap and simple, but can easily miss the one slow or broken request you actually cared about","Tail based catches the interesting cases reliably, but needs to buffer spans until the request finishes before deciding, which costs more memory and a bit more infrastructure"]
items: Head based cheap and simple, but can easily miss the one slow or broken request you actually cared about
Tail based catches the interesting cases reliably, but needs to buffer spans until the request finishes before deciding, which costs more memory and a bit more infrastructure

blocks.title: This is a real trade-off teams live with daily
blocks.content: A lot of production setups run a mix: a low flat sampling rate for normal traffic, combined with a rule that always keeps anything with an error or a latency above some threshold.
7. Real systems
7.1 Jaeger and Zipkin

Jaeger and Zipkin are dedicated tracing backends. Both do roughly the same job: receive spans, stitch them into traces by trace id, store them, and give you a UI to search traces and look at their waterfall view.

Jaeger came out of Uber and leans on Cassandra or Elasticsearch for storage at scale. Zipkin is older, came out of Twitter, and is simpler to run for smaller setups. Neither one instruments your code by itself, they just receive and display spans that something else already created.
7.2 OpenTelemetry

OpenTelemetry is where most new instrumentation work actually happens today. It's a vendor neutral standard for creating spans, propagating context, and exporting the result, and it's become the dominant way teams instrument tracing now.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351811-647905334.png
blocks.alt: An instrumented app using the OpenTelemetry SDK, exporting spans to either Jaeger or Zipkin

blocks.content: The key idea is separation. You instrument your code once against the OpenTelemetry API, and then you choose an exporter that ships the resulting spans to whichever backend you want, Jaeger, Zipkin, or a commercial option. Switch backends later and your instrumentation code doesn't change.

blocks.title: Instrument once, export anywhere
blocks.content: This is why OpenTelemetry displaced most vendor specific tracing libraries. Nobody wants to re-instrument their whole codebase just because the team decided to switch from Jaeger to a different backend.
8. Worked example: tracing a checkout request
blocks.text: 8. Worked example: tracing a checkout request

blocks.content: Back to that nine hundred millisecond checkout. With tracing wired up, that one request produced a single trace with four spans: API gateway, cart service, inventory service, and payment service.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351811-222907130.png
blocks.alt: A checkout request producing spans across the API gateway, cart service, inventory service, and payment service

blocks.title: Reading the waterfall
blocks.text: Open the trace and look at the waterfall view. The gateway span takes 40ms of overhead. The cart and inventory spans together add up to about 60ms. Then the payment span starts, and it alone runs for 800ms out of the total 900ms.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351812-242933707.png
blocks.alt: A waterfall view showing the payment span as 800ms out of a 900ms total request, far larger than the other spans

blocks.content: Without tracing, all you'd know is the checkout endpoint averaged 900ms. With it, you know exactly where to look: the payment service, not the gateway, not the cart, not inventory. That's the entire value of the tool in one picture.
9. Implementation: creating and propagating spans
Here's what actually creating a span and propagating its context looks like using the OpenTelemetry SDK for Node, inside a cart service handling an add to cart request that calls out to inventory.

On the inventory service side, the incoming traceparent header gets extracted back into a context, and any span created there automatically becomes a child of the cart service's span, same trace id, new parent.

blocks.title: Instrumentation libraries do most of this for you
blocks.content: In real projects you rarely write propagation.inject and extract by hand for every call. Auto-instrumentation packages for frameworks like Express, Fastify, or gRPC handle the header plumbing automatically. The example above is what's happening underneath.
10. The interview angle

Distributed tracing is the answer to a specific interview question: how would you debug latency in a system made of multiple services? If you're designing anything with more than one or two services talking to each other, bringing this up shows you've thought about operating the system, not just building it.

["Know the vocabulary: a trace is the whole request, a span is one unit of work, spans form a parent child tree","Know why context has to propagate across service boundaries, and that W3C Trace Context standardized how","Know that sampling exists because tracing everything doesn't scale, and that tail based sampling is how you avoid missing the errors and slow outliers that matter most","Be ready to name real tools: OpenTelemetry for instrumentation, Jaeger or Zipkin as backends"]
items: Know the vocabulary: a trace is the whole request, a span is one unit of work, spans form a parent child tree
Know why context has to propagate across service boundaries, and that W3C Trace Context standardized how
Know that sampling exists because tracing everything doesn't scale, and that tail based sampling is how you avoid missing the errors and slow outliers that matter most
Be ready to name real tools: OpenTelemetry for instrumentation, Jaeger or Zipkin as backends

blocks.title: Tie it back to the other two pillars
blocks.content: The strongest answer connects all three: metrics tell you something is slow in aggregate, logs tell you what a service was doing, and tracing tells you exactly which hop in a specific request ate the time. Mention that connection and you sound like someone who has actually run these systems.
